summary:
Problem: Power lines can start big wildfires. To stop this, power companies turn off electricity for whole towns when the wind is strong. Many people lose power, and this is dangerous for people who need medical machines at home.

Our idea: Turn off only the parts of the lines that a fire can really reach.

Innovation: We use live NASA satellite data about fires and wind forecasts. We also use NISAR radar data to see how dry the land is.

Our solution: A live map that shows where each forest fire will go. It tells every power company which parts of its lines to turn off.
details:
What it does

Power companies cut electricity to whole areas during fire weather because they cannot see which lines are truly at risk. We took the fire-behaviour models that US fire agencies rely on (Rothermel fire spread, LANDFIRE fuel maps, standard fire-weather indices) and extended them for this problem in three ways:

  • With NISAR L-band radar, which shows where fuel has still not grown back years after a fire;
  • With a model trained on 74,568 California ignitions, which estimates for every 200 m of the state and every day how likely a spark is to become a large fire;
  • With live satellite fire detections and wind forecasts matched against real transmission lines.

The result is a decision tool. For each power company it lists the line sections to switch off now, the sections to prepare, and the ones that can stay on, with a report for each. Before any fire starts, it also shows where a spark from a line would matter most and how far a fire would spread in its first hours.

What makes it different

  • It sees fuel that other open data miss. Seven and a half years after the 2018 Woolsey Fire, NISAR's radar still separates the burn scar from unburned land (detection score 0.89). Optical greenness scores 0.65 and the national fuel map 0.58.
  • It ends in a decision, not another hazard map. Each company gets an action list with the distance to the fire, the expected arrival time, and a satellite image of every section, as PDF, CSV, or GeoJSON.
  • It separates the place from the day. The map shows what the land contributes to risk and how much today's weather multiplies it, so an operator sees at once where the danger comes from.
  • It was tested the way operational models are. Trained on 2016 to 2024, checked on 2025 and 2026, with the test for NISAR written down before its fire-season data arrived.

How it works

Fire detections come from NASA VIIRS and perimeters from NIFC; wind forecasts from the US National Weather Service; fuels and terrain from LANDFIRE; weather from gridMET and NOAA HRRR; soil moisture from NASA SMAP and NISAR.

Every ten minutes the tool updates the fires, estimates where each can spread in the next 24 hours, and checks every transmission line nearby. Fire spread uses the Rothermel surface fire model with the standard fuel models. The risk model combines weather and wind gusts, terrain, fuels, what surrounds each place within a few kilometres, and the fire history. NISAR adds the state of the fuel after past fires and soil dryness at 200 m.

Results

On the 13,296 ignitions of 2025 and 2026, which the model never saw, the 15% it ranked highest held 80% of the large fires. The public fire-weather index found a third in the same number of ignitions. The model expected 87 large fires and 80 occurred. In NISAR's first fire season, its dryness signal separated the ignitions that grew better than the same measure from SMAP.
